cutout.alt: Chris Woods, MSN, APRN, FNP-C, smiling with a stethoscope

figures.alt: Labeled cross-section of a back tooth in the jaw. Labels: enamel, the hard white shell; dentin, the softer layer; pulp, the nerve room; nerve and blood vessels running down the root canals; root; gum; jawbone. Red dashed circles mark where a tooth abscess forms at the root tip and where a gum abscess forms in the gum beside the tooth.
figures.caption: Inside a tooth. A tooth abscess sits at the root tip. A gum abscess sits in the gum beside the tooth.

figures.alt: Four tooth cross-sections in order. One: acid digs a small hole in the enamel shell. Two: the hole reaches the softer dentin. Three: germs travel down to the pulp and the nerve gets angry. Four: the nerve dies and a pus pocket forms at the root tip in the jawbone.
figures.caption: From cavity to abscess, one layer at a time.

figures.alt: Three teeth side by side showing the three doors germs use: a deep cavity that reaches the pulp, a crack that splits the crown, and a deep gum pocket where a pus pocket forms beside the root.
figures.caption: Three common doors: a deep cavity, a crack, or a gum pocket.

figures.alt: Feeling map. A tooth with a deep cavity, an angry pulp, a pus pocket at the root tip, and a small bump on the gum, with pulse lines above it. Listed feelings: throb like a heartbeat, hurts to bite or tap, hot can make it roar while cold may calm it for a minute, puffy gum or a pimple-like bump, bad taste or smell. A side view of a head shows pain traveling from a lower back tooth to the ear, temple, or neck on the same side. Swelling toward the eye or neck is a red flag.
figures.caption: The feeling map: pressure, tap pain, the hot and cold flip, a gum bump, a bad taste, and pain that travels.

figures.alt: Side by side. Left, tooth abscess: a deep cavity, a dead gray nerve inside, and a pus pocket at the root tip in the bone; a dentist opens or removes the tooth. Right, gum abscess: the nerve may still be alive, and the pus pocket sits in the gum beside the root; a dentist drains and cleans the pocket. Warning strip: swelling that spreads into the face, eye, or neck is a flood, go to the ER.
figures.caption: Same germ family, different address. Spreading face or neck swelling is the ER.

stickers: Not every ache is a tooth

figures.alt: Four lookalike cards. Sinus pressure: several upper teeth ache together and it is worse when you bend over. Jaw joint: a sore hinge in front of the ear that may click or pop while the gum looks calm. Canker sore: a shallow sore on soft skin that stings with no deep throb in the bone. Ear trouble: the ear itself hurts and the teeth check out calm. Warning strip: jaw pain with chest pressure, sweating, or shortness of breath means call 911.
figures.caption: Four costumes a dental abscess can wear, and the clue for each.

stickers: The ER beats a text here

figures.alt: Red warning card titled Go to the ER or call 911, do not text first. Six red flags with icons: trouble breathing, cannot swallow spit, floor of the mouth rising, neck hard or swelling, eye swelling shut, and high fever with confusion.
figures.caption: If you see any of these, skip the text. Go to the ER or call 911.

figures.alt: Four care steps on a dotted path. One, find the source: a dentist checks the tooth and takes an X-ray. Two, let the pus out: open the tooth, or a small cut in the gum drains it. Three, fix the source: a root canal cleans and seals the nerve room, or the tooth is removed if it cannot be saved. Four, helper medicine if it fits: it calms germs as a bridge and is not the repair. Steps one to three are the dentist, and step four never replaces them.
figures.caption: Source first. A helper medicine is a bridge, not the repair.

figures.alt: Who does what. Dentist, fixes the tooth: exam and X-ray, opens and drains the pocket, root canal or removes the tooth. Text visit with Chris, the bridge: asks the red-flag questions, symptom care plan for tonight, helper medicine only if it fits, points you to the right door. ER, the airway door: trouble breathing or swallowing, swelling spreading in the face or neck.
figures.caption: Three doors. Each one has a different job.

figures.alt: A loop of red arrows around a tooth with a dead nerve and a pus pocket at the root tip. Source still open, from a dead nerve, a crack, or a gum pocket. Germs grow back. The pocket refills and the throb returns. A helper calms it for a while. Then back to the start. A blue bar below reads: break the loop, a dentist fixes the source.
figures.caption: The comeback loop keeps spinning until a dentist fixes the source.

figures.alt: Four myth and fact pairs. Myth: if it drains, it is over. Fact: a drain is a pressure valve and the source is still open. Myth: no pain means it healed. Fact: a dead nerve can go quiet while germs keep working. Myth: salt water will cure it. Fact: a rinse is comfort, not a repair. Myth: a text visit replaces a dentist. Fact: text can be a bridge, and a dentist fixes the tooth.
figures.caption: Four myths I hear every week, and the facts that beat them.
